passage: I'm Manjula, and I still remember the day Lalit sat down on the corridor floor outside the exam hall. His face had gone grey, and he was gasping. "I can't breathe. Something's wrong. I'm dying." A crowd started to gather. I asked them to give us space. Then I sat down next to him, close but not touching, and spoke slowly. "I'm here. This is a wave of panic. It's horrible, but it will pass. Breathe out slowly with me." I didn't argue with him or say, "You're fine." I just kept saying it would pass, and it did, after a few long minutes. When it happened again the next month, I told him gently, "I think you should see a doctor or a counsellor about this." He went. I went with him.

qa.q: Where did Lalit sit down when the panic started?
qa.a: On the corridor floor outside the exam hall.

qa.q: What did Lalit believe was happening during the attack?
qa.a: He felt terrified, believing something was wrong and that he was dying.

qa.q: Which of Manjula's choices helped Lalit most in the moment?
qa.a: Manjula cleared the crowd, sat close without touching, spoke slowly, and kept reminding him it would pass.

qa.q: How might the gathering crowd have made things worse for Lalit?
qa.a: Being crowded and stared at could have made him feel more trapped and frightened.

grounding: It shows a calm companion who stays close, speaks slowly, reminds the person it will pass, does not crowd or argue, and later encourages professional help.

passage: Coach's note, district meet Before the 400m final, Tejas was found in the changing room, doubled over, gasping and shaking. He said, "My heart, something's badly wrong." His teammates were crowding round, all talking at once. What I did: I asked the others to wait outside. I sat a little distance from him and spoke slowly. "Tejas, I'm here. This is panic. It's frightening, and it will pass." He said, "No, it won't." I didn't argue. I kept my voice low and breathed slowly where he could see me. After a few minutes his breathing eased. Afterwards I told his parents. If it happens again, I've suggested they see a doctor or a counsellor together. He didn't run the final. He's running next month. - Rajni, athletics coach

passage:
Wednesday
Right after the chemistry exam, Vandana suddenly grabbed the corridor railing. She was breathing fast and said, "My heart, I can't, something's wrong." People started crowding round. I asked them to give us space, and they moved back.
I stayed next to her but didn't hold her. I talked slowly. "I'm here. You're safe. This will pass." I didn't argue when she said she was dying; I just kept saying it will pass and counted slow breaths out loud. After a few minutes her shoulders dropped.
Later, over samosas, she said this was the third time this month. I told her that's worth a proper check, and asked if she'd tell her mum and see the school counsellor. She said she would, tomorrow.
Eshaan

passage: At the temple fair in their village, the crowd pressed in around the drummers. Sarika, fifteen, suddenly clutched Usha's arm. "I can't breathe, my heart, I'm going to faint." It was the second time since Holi. Usha didn't argue or tell her she was being silly. She led her slowly away to the quiet steps behind the old well, and asked their cousins to stay back. She sat beside her, close but not touching, and spoke slowly. "It's scary, but it will pass. I'm right here." After a while Sarika's breathing slowed. Walking home past the fields, Usha said gently, "This has happened twice now. Will you tell your mother, and see the doctor at the health centre?" Sarika nodded.

passage:
In the changing room at the swimming club in Lisbon, Oskar suddenly sat down hard on the bench. His breath came fast and shallow. "I can't breathe. Something's wrong."
Layla didn't crowd him or call everyone over. She crouched a little distance away and spoke slowly. "I'm right here, Oskar. This is a wave. It feels awful, and it will pass."
"It won't," he gasped.
She didn't argue. "Okay. Just feel your feet on the floor. Breathe out slowly with me." She breathed out, long and steady. He tried to copy her.
Gradually his shoulders dropped. He wiped his face.
Walking home, Layla said, "Has this happened before?"
"Twice."
"Then will you tell your dad tonight and see the doctor? Or the school counsellor? You shouldn't carry it alone." Oskar nodded, and she walked him to his door.

qa.q: Where was Oskar when the attack started?
qa.a: In the changing room at the swimming club.

qa.q: How was Oskar feeling when he sat down hard on the bench?
qa.a: He was frightened and panicky, breathing fast and sure something was wrong.

qa.q: Which of Layla's choices helped most, and why?
qa.a: Staying close without crowding, speaking slowly, saying it would pass without arguing, then urging a doctor or counsellor because it had happened before.

qa.q: What is it like for Oskar to have Layla there?
qa.a: He likely feels less alone and a bit calmer, able to copy her steady breathing instead of being swept away by fear.

grounding: Layla stays close, speaks slowly and reminds Oskar the panic will pass without arguing or crowding, then encourages him to see a doctor or counsellor since it has recurred.
